learning: If slalom line loss falls below 1 with body_length 0.12, keep the shorter body and tune base_speed for completion time. If slalom line loss is unchanged or worse, yaw inertia is not the limiter; the next geometry test is wheel_track 0.10 with kp rescaled to about 2.7 (kp is scaled by the 0.12/0.10 yaw-gain ratio), not a further body change.
notes: Race 7 controller held unchanged with the Builder's body_length 0.12 m geometry. Only the body changes, so the slalom result isolates yaw inertia. If oscillation rises above 0.35 on oval, tune kd before any further geometry change.
rationale: Race 7 (636.91) is the best measured design: five 16 mm sensors at x = -0.03 to +0.03, y = 0.06, body_length 0.18, kp 3.2, kd 0.6, base_speed 0.95, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2]. Oval finished 20/20 and s-bend 16/20, but slalom finished 0/20 with 1.2 line-loss events per run and max_error at 0.063. The Builder's proposal changes only body_length from 0.18 to 0.12 m. Under the agreed rule, slalom line loss at 1 or more with max_error at the limit after gain tuning points to the platform, so this is the geometry test. Yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12, so the shorter body cuts it by about 38 percent. The contract says body_length has no direct dynamics effect, but it does enter yaw inertia, so this is a real, single-variable test. I keep the race 7 controller unchanged, so any change in slalom is attributable to body_length. Expected result, not measured: slalom line loss below 1 with max_error below 0.06, oval and s-bend close to race 7. If oval steering_oscillation rises above 0.35 with the same gains, the faster yaw response needs kd tuning before any further geometry change, as the Builder's own rule states.
